items.name: narration
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular geography YouTube Shorts channel. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: brisk and curious, with natural emphasis, a short comic pause before each punchline, and a warmer, slightly slower, proud tone for the line about ordinary Americans. Chars voices funny cartoon characters, short and punchy.
lines: Narrator
You know the Statue of Liberty. But almost twenty years before New York... Egypt said no to her.
Narrator
Rewind to the eighteen-sixties. Bar-tol-dee pitches Egypt a giant woman with a light, for the new Suez Canal.
Chars
[bored, regal, unimpressed royal] Magnificent. Too expensive. No.
Narrator
So Bar-tol-dee reworks it. Same big lady... New continent.
Narrator
So who pays? France pays for the statue. America pays for the stand.
Narrator
By eighteen eighty-four, she's finished in Paris, poking above the rooftops. Imagine that as your neighbour.
Narrator
Her iron skeleton? Designed by Gustave Eiffel. Yes... that Eiffel.
Narrator
Then Paris takes her apart. About three hundred and fifty pieces. Two hundred and fourteen crates. Across the Atlantic.
Narrator
Spoiler: New York's stand fund has about three thousand dollars.
Chars
[muffled, echoing from inside a wooden box, polite and confused lady] Hello? Where do I stand?
Narrator
So how do you finish her?
Narrator
Newspaper owner Joseph Pulitzer promises to print every donor's name. Any amount.
Narrator
About a hundred and twenty thousand people chip in. Most gifts are under one dollar.
Narrator
France gave her a body. Ordinary Americans... gave her somewhere to stand.
Narrator
She's unveiled on October twenty-eighth, eighteen eighty-six. A hundred and forty years ago.
Narrator
And the twist? Her island is New York. The water around it?... New Jersey.
Chars
[grumpy, deadpan, flat tough-guy] Lovely statue. Standing in my water.
Narrator
Pitched to Egypt. Built in Paris. Paid in coins. Standing in New Jersey. Very American.
Narrator
This is Bhoogol. Follow for more Geography Fun Facts.
